atoms.text: A Ti-6Al-4V hydraulic manifold for ground support equipment is built on a single-laser powder bed fusion machine in a batch of four units, with a required density above 99.9% and a proof pressure of 52 MPa. Every build starts with 100% virgin Grade 23 powder, and the powder left in the chamber and overflow bins after the job is discarded because no reuse specification exists. The chamber is purged with argon at a constant 40 L/min for the whole 38-hour build and the exhaust is vented without recovery, so about 90 m³ of argon is consumed per build. Parts are oriented with large overhangs and held by dense solid supports, which bring the support mass to about 35% of the part mass and increase the machining stock. The chiller and recoater heater run continuously, including the 14 hours of idle time between jobs, and energy use is not metered per build. Oxygen level, filter pressure, and melt pool signals are not logged, so a failed build is found only after CT inspection and two of the four manifolds are scrapped. Scrapped parts, cut-off supports, and the used build plate go to general metal waste, and the spent filter cartridge is disposed of as hazardous waste without any metal recovery. Virgin powder is air-freighted from an overseas atomizer in 10 kg containers, and each build is stress relieved in a separate cycle at a contract furnace 400 km away.

A Ti-6Al-4V hydraulic manifold for ground support equipment is built on a single-laser powder bed fusion machine in a batch of four units, with a required density above 99.9% and a proof pressure of 52 MPa. Each build uses a blend of recycled and virgin Grade 23 powder, in which overflow powder is sieved at 63 µm under inert conditions, tracked by lot, and capped at ten reuse cycles. A blend is released only after oxygen, nitrogen, and particle size distribution checks. The chamber is purged to 0.1% oxygen and then held with argon at 12 L/min, and a closed-loop recirculation unit with filtration returns most of the gas, cutting consumption to about 25 m³ per build. Parts are tilted to reduce overhangs and are held by lattice supports with 60% lower mass, which brings support mass to about 12% of the part mass and reduces the machining stock. The chiller and preheater switch to standby after job completion, and energy meters record kWh per build for comparison with a target value. In-situ monitoring logs oxygen, filter differential pressure, and melt pool emission, so a build that drifts out of limits is paused early and all four manifolds pass CT inspection on the first run. Cut-off supports, rejected parts, and the retired build plate are collected as segregated titanium scrap and returned to the powder supplier for remelting, while spent filters go to a certified recycler that recovers the metal. Powder is bought in 50 kg lots from an atomizer within 300 km, and stress relief runs in an on-site furnace together with other builds to fill the furnace load.

An Inconel 718 fuel nozzle swirler for an industrial gas turbine is produced in a series of 24 pieces on a four-laser powder bed fusion system, with a required density above 99.8% and low-cycle fatigue performance equal to wrought-derived specifications. Each build is loaded with 100% virgin powder at 15-45 µm, and the remaining powder is treated as contaminated and sent for disposal after one use. Argon is supplied at a fixed 50 L/min from bulk cylinders, the chamber is flushed three times before every build, and all exhaust is released to the building ventilation. Process parameters are set at the maximum laser power to shorten the build, which causes heavy spatter and a 15% rejection rate from lack-of-fusion porosity. Spatter and soot are not separated from the powder bed, so contamination is found only at final inspection. Stress relief, hot isostatic pressing, and solution and aging treatments are run as three separate furnace cycles at different external vendors, with partial loads in each. Wire-cut removal from the plate uses fresh dielectric fluid for every batch, and the used fluid and the sludge are sent to waste. Rejected swirlers and machining chips are mixed with other alloys and sold as low-grade scrap, and the powder lots are not traceable to a specific part.

An Inconel 718 fuel nozzle swirler for an industrial gas turbine is produced in a series of 24 pieces on a four-laser powder bed fusion system, with a required density above 99.8% and low-cycle fatigue performance equal to wrought-derived specifications. Builds use a blend of at most 70% reused powder at 15-45 µm, which is sieved after each job, sampled for oxygen content and flowability, and linked to the part serial numbers. Argon is supplied from a bulk tank at 15 L/min after a single evacuation and refill sequence, and a recirculation loop with a hot-getter or filter stage recovers most of the gas. Process parameters are optimized to moderate laser power and lower scan speed, which reduces spatter and lowers the rejection rate from lack-of-fusion porosity to about 3%. Spatter is removed by the cross-flow system and filtered, and the filter loading is monitored so that gas velocity at the build plate stays within limits. Stress relief, hot isostatic pressing, and solution and aging treatments are combined into one planned sequence at a single vendor with fully loaded furnaces, which removes two transport legs. Wire-cut removal uses a filtered dielectric fluid that is reused over many batches, and the sludge is collected for metal recovery. Rejected swirlers and machining chips are sorted by alloy, labelled, and returned to the supplier for remelting into new powder-grade feedstock.

An AlSi10Mg liquid-cooled heat exchanger for power electronics is manufactured in a pilot batch of ten units on a powder bed fusion machine, with a helium leak rate below 1e-8 mbar·L/s at 1 MPa and a thermal conductivity above 120 W/m·K after stress relief. Each build uses new powder from freshly opened drums, and used powder is discarded because humidity pickup is assumed to make it unusable. Powder drums are stored in an uncontrolled warehouse, so moisture content varies and is not measured before loading. The chamber is flooded with argon at 45 L/min, even though nitrogen is acceptable for this alloy, and the gas is vented after one pass. Thin internal channels are built vertically with dense support material that must be removed by long machining and manual rework, which creates scrap chips and contaminated coolant. The build plate is heated to 200 °C for the full duration, and the machine runs a fixed 24-hour cycle regardless of the actual layer count. Leak testing is done only on finished parts, and 4 of 10 exchangers are rejected for porosity and leaking channels. Rejected parts, support chips, and loose powder are discarded as mixed aluminum waste, and the rest of the batch is shipped by express courier to the customer in single-use foam packaging.

An AlSi10Mg liquid-cooled heat exchanger for power electronics is manufactured in a pilot batch of ten units on a powder bed fusion machine, with a helium leak rate below 1e-8 mbar·L/s at 1 MPa and a thermal conductivity above 120 W/m·K after stress relief. Powder is reclaimed after each build, sieved, dried in a vacuum oven, and checked for moisture below 0.1% before reuse, with a maximum of eight cycles per lot. Drums are stored in a humidity-controlled area at below 40% relative humidity, and the lot moisture data is recorded before each build. The chamber is inerted with nitrogen, which is acceptable for this alloy, at 20 L/min, and a recirculation unit with filtration returns most of the gas to the chamber. Internal channels are redesigned at self-supporting angles of 45° or more, which removes most support material and shortens the machining and manual rework. The build plate preheat is set to 150 °C, and job duration is matched to the layer count, so the machine does not run idle at temperature. Layer-wise imaging and melt pool monitoring identify porosity-prone regions, and a leak test of the channels on the as-built part before stress relief lets nonconforming parts be stopped early, giving 9 of 10 passing parts. Support chips, rejected parts, and powder residues are segregated as aluminum scrap and sent for remelting, and the finished exchangers are shipped in returnable reusable crates by consolidated road freight.

A 316L stainless steel pump impeller of 180 mm diameter is produced as a single spare part on demand for a chemical plant, with a density above 99.5%, a yield strength above 450 MPa, and a surface roughness of Ra 3.2 µm on the flow surfaces. The part is built alone on a full-size 400 × 400 mm plate, so more than 90% of the build area is unused and a full powder bed of 60 kg is loaded for the one job. After the 22-hour build, all remaining powder is dumped as waste instead of being returned to stock. The machine is preheated and flushed with argon at 40 L/min for 3 hours before the first layer, then continues to run at the same flow rate until the plate cools. The impeller is built with a fixed 30 µm layer thickness and full contour passes, with no optimization of the blade geometry, which yields a part mass 40% higher than needed. Residual stresses are not relieved before cutting from the plate, and the impeller warps beyond tolerance, so a second one is built to replace it. Surface finishing is performed by abrasive blasting and manual grinding with disposable media, and spent media is landfilled. No energy, gas, or powder data are recorded, and the original and scrap impellers are shipped by overnight air freight from the service bureau to the plant.

A 316L stainless steel pump impeller of 180 mm diameter is produced as a single spare part on demand for a chemical plant, with a density above 99.5%, a yield strength above 450 MPa, and a surface roughness of Ra 3.2 µm on the flow surfaces. The job is combined with other small orders from the service bureau on a 250 × 250 mm plate, so the build area is above 70% utilized, and the powder bed is sized to the job at about 18 kg. After the 22-hour build, the remaining powder is sieved, logged by lot, and returned to stock for later use. The chamber is flushed to a defined oxygen threshold and is then held at 10 L/min with gas recirculation, and the argon supply is shut down once the plate temperature allows safe opening. Blade thickness is reduced by topology analysis against the pump duty point, which lowers the part mass by about 20% and shortens the build time, and the layer thickness of 60 µm is used for the core with finer contour settings at the surfaces. Residual stresses are relieved on the plate before cutting, and the impeller stays within tolerance on the first build, which avoids a repeat. Surface finishing uses vibratory finishing with a recirculated media and a filtered water loop, and spent media and sludge are collected for metal recovery. Powder use, gas volume, and energy per build are recorded, and the finished part is shipped by road from a service bureau within 200 km in reusable packaging.

A maraging steel 1.2709 injection mold insert with conformal cooling channels is built for a plastics molding line, with a target hardness of 52-54 HRC after aging and a channel position tolerance of ±0.15 mm. The insert is built as a solid block with the cooling channels designed on a standard layout that does not follow the cavity, which results in 1.4 times the material mass needed. Virgin powder fills the machine for each build, and the used powder is placed in drums without sieving or labelling and stored until it is later disposed of as mixed material. The chamber is flushed with argon at 35 L/min for the full 30-hour build, and the nozzle and filter are replaced after each job whether or not their loading requires it. The preheated plate and the laser system run on a fixed schedule even when the machine waits for operators between shifts. The insert is aged at 490 °C in a small furnace with a single part load for 6 hours, and the unused furnace volume is heated as well. Powder trapped in channels is removed by compressed air and the loose powder is swept into general waste. The channels are checked only by visual inspection at the end, and a blocked channel on the first insert requires the entire insert to be scrapped and rebuilt.

A maraging steel 1.2709 injection mold insert with conformal cooling channels is built for a plastics molding line, with a target hardness of 52-54 HRC after aging and a channel position tolerance of ±0.15 mm. The cooling channels follow the cavity contour at a constant distance, and the insert body is partly hollowed with a lattice infill, which reduces the material mass by about 25% compared with a solid block. The build uses a blend of reclaimed and virgin powder, where used powder is sieved, labelled by lot and reused for up to ten cycles after chemical and particle size checks. The chamber is flushed to a set oxygen limit and held at 12 L/min with recirculation, and the nozzle and filter are replaced based on measured differential pressure rather than fixed intervals. The machine switches the preheat and laser to standby when the job is finished or waits for operators, and the energy use per build is logged. Several inserts and other small parts are aged together at 490 °C in a full furnace load, which uses the heated volume efficiently. Powder trapped in channels is removed by vacuum extraction with an inert collection vessel, and the recovered powder is returned to the sieving station. Channel openness is verified by a flow test and borescope inspection before aging, so a blocked channel is found early, and a single re-print is limited to a small sub-section.

A CuCrZr heat sink for a resistance welding electrode holder is built in a batch of six on a powder bed fusion machine, with an electrical conductivity of at least 80% IACS after precipitation hardening and a density above 99%. High-reflectivity copper powder is bought as virgin material for each build, and any powder remaining after the job is classified as scrap because of fear of oxygen pickup, although it is not measured. Argon is supplied at 50 L/min and the chamber oxygen is allowed to reach 1,000 ppm before the build starts, which increases oxide inclusions and reduces conductivity. The build uses maximum laser power with long exposure times to compensate for the heat conducted away, and about 20% of the parts fail the conductivity and density checks. The parts are built tightly packed with dense supports, and the support removal by wire erosion leaves large amounts of copper sludge that is discarded with the dielectric. Heat treatment is performed in a vacuum furnace with a continuous nitrogen backfill and a partial load of two parts. The machine, chiller, and extraction fan stay on during weekends and between builds. The rejected heat sinks and sludge are placed in general metal waste, and the powder is delivered by truck from a supplier 1,200 km away in single-use drums.

A CuCrZr heat sink for a resistance welding electrode holder is built in a batch of six on a powder bed fusion machine, with an electrical conductivity of at least 80% IACS after precipitation hardening and a density above 99%. Copper alloy powder is reclaimed after each build, sieved under inert conditions, and tested for oxygen content, so lots with measured oxygen below the limit return to a blend with virgin powder. Argon is supplied at 18 L/min after the chamber reaches 100 ppm oxygen, and the build is held under that limit with a recirculation loop, which reduces oxide inclusions and supports the conductivity requirement. Process parameters are tuned using a short parameter study with moderate laser power and a preheated plate, and the failure rate on conductivity and density checks falls to about 4%. The parts are arranged with adequate spacing, built with minimal supports, and removed by wire erosion with a filtered dielectric, so the copper sludge is collected and sent for metal recovery. Aging is done in a vacuum furnace with all six parts and other copper alloy parts in the same load, which reduces the number of heating cycles. The machine, chiller, and extraction fan go to standby between builds and on weekends. Rejected heat sinks and chips are segregated by alloy and returned for remelting, and the powder is delivered in returnable containers from a supplier within 250 km.

An Inconel 625 valve body of 300 mm height for a chemical processing line is built in a batch of four on a large-format powder bed fusion machine, with a density above 99.8% and a corrosion resistance equivalent to wrought material. Fresh powder is loaded for each build, and the 200 kg of remaining powder in the chamber and overflow bins is regarded as waste because the facility has no sieving or storage system. The chamber is purged with argon at 60 L/min throughout the 70-hour build, and the gas is vented, which consumes about 250 m³ per job. The valve bodies are built horizontally with a large flat footprint and solid supports, so the build height is shorter but the support volume is about 40% of the part volume. Process monitoring is not applied, so a recoater blade crash at hour 45 goes unnoticed and affects the remaining layers, and all four parts are rejected after final inspection. The same heat treatment cycle is repeated for each part individually in a vendor furnace, and the finished machining uses flood coolant that is replaced every few weeks. Machining chips from Inconel 625 are mixed with stainless steel swarf and sent as low-value scrap. The machine, extraction unit, and chiller operate at full output through the entire job, including the recoating and cooling periods, and no energy values are reported.

An Inconel 625 valve body of 300 mm height for a chemical processing line is built in a batch of four on a large-format powder bed fusion machine, with a density above 99.8% and a corrosion resistance equivalent to wrought material. The 200 kg of powder left in the chamber and overflow bins is vacuumed into a closed handling system, sieved at 63 µm, and returned to a storage vessel under argon with lot and cycle records. Each following build uses a blend with at least 50% reclaimed powder, based on chemistry and particle size results. The chamber is purged to a specified oxygen level, and the build is held at 20 L/min with gas recirculation, which brings the total argon use to about 80 m³ per job. The valve bodies are oriented vertically at an angle to reduce unsupported surfaces, with lightweight supports that are about 15% of the part volume, which increases build height but reduces the support removal work. Layer imaging and recoater monitoring detect a blade fault at hour 45, the build is paused, the blade is replaced, and all four parts are completed and pass inspection. One planned heat treatment cycle covers all four parts, and the finishing machining uses minimum-quantity lubrication or a filtered coolant that is reused and tested. Inconel 625 chips are collected separately by alloy and sent to the supplier for remelting. The machine, extraction unit, and chiller use reduced power modes during recoating and cooling periods, and the energy use per build is reported.

A series of 200 17-4 PH stainless steel robotic gripper fingers is produced on a four-laser powder bed fusion system for an automotive assembly line, with a tensile strength above 1,000 MPa after H1025 aging and a mass limit of 85 g per finger. The fingers are designed as solid bodies with a conventional geometry, and the mass is 130 g each, which requires about 50% more powder per part than the target design. Each plate is filled with fingers at a low packing density of 30%, so 200 pieces need 14 builds. Every build starts with virgin powder, and the powder left after the build is stored in open containers where it absorbs moisture and dust, and it is eventually disposed of. The chamber is flushed with nitrogen or argon at 45 L/min throughout every 26-hour job, and the gas is released after use. The parts are cut from the plate with a band saw, which generates chips and requires cutting fluid, and the plates are ground and discarded after a single use. Quality control is performed by sampling the first and last part of the series, and drift in the process across the 14 builds results in 12% of the fingers being out of tolerance. The out-of-tolerance fingers are dumped as general waste, and the series is delivered in single-use packaging by multiple partial shipments.

A series of 200 17-4 PH stainless steel robotic gripper fingers is produced on a four-laser powder bed fusion system for an automotive assembly line, with a tensile strength above 1,000 MPa after H1025 aging and a mass limit of 85 g per finger. The fingers are redesigned with internal lattice and topology-optimized ribs, which brings the mass to 80 g each and reduces the powder demand per part by about 40%. Each plate is filled with fingers at 70% packing density, and the series is completed in 6 builds. Builds use a blend of reclaimed and virgin powder, and the remaining powder is sieved, stored in sealed containers under inert gas with a desiccant, and tracked by lot and cycle count. The chamber is purged to a defined oxygen limit and is held at 14 L/min with a recirculation unit, so the gas volume per finger drops significantly compared with a standard run. The parts are cut from the plate by wire erosion, which saves plate material, and the plates are resurfaced and reused up to a set minimum thickness. Quality control uses in-situ melt pool and layer monitoring in every build, together with density and tensile coupons placed in each plate, and the process remains stable, with fewer than 2% of the fingers out of tolerance. Out-of-tolerance fingers and chips are sorted by alloy and returned for remelting, and the series is delivered in returnable crates in a single consolidated shipment.
